title: Tables or Documents
summary: Larder, a meal-kit app, has orders, recipes, sessions and van GPS pings. One database shape doesn't fit them all — learn the four families and what each trades away.

goals.text: Model data as tables linked by keys, and query it with joins
See why multi-table transactions matter for money
Recognise when a document fits better than six tables
Know what key-value and wide-column stores are for
Pick a store per access pattern, not per fashion

steps.title: Where should Larder's data live?
body: Larder ships meal kits. Its API juggles four very different kinds of data: orders (money!), recipes (rich, nested content), sessions (tiny, hot, short-lived) and GPS pings from delivery vans (endless append-only stream).
Before picking a database, ask what shape the data has and how it will be read and written. Databases differ mostly in what they make easy — and what they make you do yourself.

steps.title: Relational: rows, columns and keys
body: A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed set of typed columns. Each row has a primary key; rows point at other rows through foreign keys — an order row stores customer_id, an order item stores order_id.
Each fact lives in exactly one place (normalised): change a customer's email once and every order sees it. The database enforces the schema, so bad data is rejected at the door.
changes: + Postgres with customers, orders, order_items, inventory

steps.title: Joins reassemble the picture
body: Because facts are split across tables, reads put them back together with a join: one SQL statement matches orders to their customer and items using the keys.
You can ask questions nobody planned for — “revenue per city last week” — without changing how data is stored. That flexibility at query time is the relational model's superpower.

card.title: One query, three tables
lines: JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
= one round trip, one consistent answer

steps.title: All-or-nothing checkout
body: Checkout touches three tables: decrement stock, insert the order, insert its items. A transaction wraps them so they commit together or not at all — a crash halfway can't leave stock taken with no order.
This is ACID: Atomic, Consistent (constraints hold), Isolated (concurrent checkouts don't see each other's half-done work), Durable (committed means on disk).

callout.text: For money, inventory and anything with invariants, multi-row transactions are worth a lot. Rebuilding them in application code is hard and error-prone.

changes: ~ Checkout writes 4 rows in one transaction

card.title: Checkout = one transaction
lines: = all four changes land, or none do

steps.title: Recipes don't want to be tables
body: A recipe is one nested thing: a title, an ordered list of steps, ingredients with quantities, nutrition, tags, photos. Normalised, it becomes six tables — and every recipe page is a six-way join stitching ~60 rows back together.
Worse, the content team adds fields every week (“allergens”, “wine pairing”). Each one is a schema migration on a growing table. The data's shape fights the model.

card.title: Showing one recipe
lines: # a recipe is one nested thing, stored as six tables

steps.title: Document store: keep it together
body: A document database stores each recipe as one JSON-like document, nested lists and all. Reading a recipe is a single lookup by id — the data is already in the shape the page needs.
The schema is flexible: a new field is just a new key in new documents. Because each document is self-contained, the store can spread documents across many machines more easily.
The cost: joins across documents are limited, and atomic updates are usually per document. That's fine for recipes — and exactly why orders stay in Postgres.

callout.text: “Schemaless” means the schema lives in your code instead. Old documents keep old shapes — readers must handle both.

card.title: One recipe = one document
lines: # a new field is just a new key — no migration

steps.title: Key-value: fastest when you know the key
body: Sessions and carts are read on every request, always by their id. A key-value store is a distributed hash map: put(key, value), get(key), done. Lookups take about a millisecond and capacity grows by adding nodes.
The value is opaque to the store. You can't ask “which carts contain salmon?” — if you need that question, you need a different store (or a second copy of the data).

card.title: Key-value: a giant hash map
lines: # the store can't look inside the value

steps.title: Wide-column: built for floods of writes
body: Each van reports its position every 10 seconds — millions of small writes a day that are only ever read as “the trail of delivery X”. A wide-column store groups rows by a partition key (order_id) and keeps them sorted by a clustering key (event_time).
Writes spread evenly over many nodes and are cheap appends. The price: you design each table around one query up front, and joins and cross-partition transactions are essentially off the table.
changes: + Wide-column store fed by delivery vans

card.title: Wide-column: rows grouped by key
lines: partition: order_id  →  all events of one delivery
clustering: event_time  →  kept sorted on disk
= huge write volume, spread over many nodes
! design tables around the queries you'll run

Larder now runs four stores — and pays for it: four things to operate, back up and monitor, plus data that must be kept in sync between them.

callout.text: Polyglot persistence multiplies operational work. Each extra store must earn its place with a real access pattern.

changes: ~ Each store owns one kind of data

steps.title: Shape and access pattern decide
body:
• Relational: normalised tables, joins, multi-row ACID transactions. The safe default.
  • Document: self-contained nested records read whole; flexible schema, weaker joins.
  • Key-value: get/put by key at huge rates; no queries on the value.
  • Wide-column: write-heavy data partitioned by key, tables designed per query.
Start with one relational database. Add a specialised store only when a concrete workload outgrows it.

card.title: Choose by access pattern
lines: lookups by one key, huge rate → **key-value**
= default to relational; add others for a reason
